newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria to hold local elections on October 23.
newsitem.headline: Algeria to hold local elections on October 23.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual announced on Wednesday that local elections would be held on October 23, a final step in restoring elected institutions which crumbled amid violence between Moslem militants and security forces.
A presidential statement carried by the official Algerian news agency APS set the date and announced the setting up of a poll watchdog.
It was preceded by reports of more massacres in remote villages, underscoring the country's continuing bloodshed.
Voters will elect mayors and local councils in the North African country's 48 main cities and more than 1,500 towns and villages.
Zeroual, who held talks with opposition leaders before setting the election date, signed an order to create the watchdog in which legal opposition groups will be represented.
The October vote will be the fourth plural election since 1995 when Algerians voted for the first time to elect the head of state from among four contenders.

It will be the first poll since Abassi Madani, leader of the outlawed radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), was released from jail. It was not clear whether the newly freed FIS chief would call on supporters to boycott the poll or endorse it as a goodwill gesture towards the authorities.

It was the FIS landslide lead in Algeria's first multi-party general election that caused the authorities to scrap the poll in January 1992 and two months later to ban the party. Violence rapidly erupted and an estimated 60,000 people have since died.
The authorities freed Madani last week midway through the 12-year prison term imposed on him in July 1992 for threatening state security.
Zeroual, a former army general, won the presidential poll on pledges to rebuild political institutions and restore peace in the oil and gas producing country.

But the bloodshed has continued unabated. More than 400 civilians have been killed since last month's general election in which 103 moderate Islamist politicians won seats in the 380-member National Assembly (lower house).
Moslem rebels killed 47 people, mostly by cuttting their throats, in two attacks south of Algiers, an Algerian newspaper said on Wednesday.
Le Matin daily said 38 were slaughtered in one attack and nine in another in Blida province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of the Algerian capital, overnight on Sunday-Monday.
The October ballot will also complete the shape of a new parliament as elected local authorities will vote on 144 members of the country's Council of the Nation, the upper house.
The president will appoint the other third from the ranks of leading personalities, union officials and other professionals.
According to the constitution adopted last November, the National Assembly, or lower house, and the Council of the Nation form the parliament.
Algeria elected a multi-party National Assembly last month with MPs from 10 political parties plus 11 independents.
The constitution created a complex balance of power between the two houses as part of Algerian leaders' efforts to ensure stability in the country of 29 million people.
While the lower house can topple the government by rejecting its programme, the upper house's leader is entitled to replace the president in case he is impeached or incapacitated.
Algeria has been without a parliament since 1992 when the authorities cancelled the general election.
Authorities later ousted most of the local authorities elected in 1990 in Algeria's first multi-party election which had been dominated by radical Moslem militants.
They accused the militants of turning town halls into a "spider's web" for the guerrillas.
